questions.question: What is the most widely used distributed version control system?
questions.explanation: Git is the most popular distributed version control system, used by millions of developers worldwide for tracking code changes.

questions.question: What Git command creates a new independent line of development?
questions.explanation: git branch creates a new branch, allowing developers to work on features or fixes independently from the main codebase.

questions.question: What operation combines changes from one branch into another?
questions.explanation: Merge combines changes from one branch into another, integrating different lines of development.

questions.question: What Git command downloads a copy of a remote repository?
questions.explanation: git clone creates a local copy of a remote repository, including all files, branches, and commit history.

questions.question: Which operation rewrites commit history by moving commits to a new base?
questions.explanation: Rebase moves or combines commits to a new base commit, creating a linear history without merge commits.

questions.question: What is a request to merge code changes from one branch to another called?
questions.explanation: A Pull Request is a GitHub feature that lets you notify others about changes you've pushed to a branch, requesting review and merge.

questions.question: What situation occurs when two branches modify the same part of code differently?
questions.explanation: A Merge Conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically resolve differences between two commits, requiring manual resolution.

questions.question: What workflow uses short-lived feature branches merged frequently?
questions.explanation: Trunk-Based Development involves developers working in short-lived feature branches that are frequently merged back to the main trunk.

questions.question: What Git command temporarily saves changes without committing?
questions.explanation: git stash temporarily stores modified tracked files, allowing you to switch branches without committing incomplete work.

questions.question: What creates a named reference to a specific commit?
questions.explanation: A Tag is a reference to a specific commit, typically used to mark release points like v1.0, v2.0, etc.

questions.question: Which Git command uploads local commits to a remote repository?
questions.explanation: git push sends committed changes from the local repository to the corresponding remote branch.

questions.question: Which Git command downloads changes from a remote and integrates them into the current branch?
questions.explanation: git pull fetches remote changes and merges them into the current local branch in one step.

questions.question: Which Git command stages modified files for the next commit?
questions.explanation: git add moves changes from the working directory into the staging area, preparing them for the next commit.

questions.question: Which Git command displays the commit history of a repository?
questions.explanation: git log lists the commit history, showing authors, dates, and commit messages in reverse chronological order.

questions.question: Which Git command shows the working tree status, including staged and untracked changes?
questions.explanation: git status reports which files are staged, modified, or untracked relative to the current branch.

questions.question: Which file tells Git which files or directories to ignore?
questions.explanation: The .gitignore file lists patterns of files and directories Git should exclude from tracking.

questions.question: Which Git command creates a new commit that reverses the changes of a previous commit?
questions.explanation: git revert safely undoes a commit by creating a new commit with the inverse changes, preserving history.

questions.question: Which Git command applies a specific existing commit onto the current branch?
questions.explanation: git cherry-pick copies the changes from a single named commit and applies them as a new commit on the current branch.

questions.question: Which branching model uses dedicated develop, release, and hotfix branches alongside main/master?
questions.explanation: GitFlow defines a strict branching model with feature, develop, release, and hotfix branches supporting versioned releases.

questions.question: Which hosting platform popularized the pull request and fork-based collaboration workflow?
questions.explanation: GitHub popularized pull requests and the fork-and-pull model for open-source and team collaboration.

questions.question: In Git, what does HEAD refer to?
options: A pointer to the currently checked-out commit or branch
The first commit in the repository
A special tag marking the latest release
questions.explanation: HEAD is a symbolic reference pointing to the currently checked-out branch tip or commit.

questions.question: Which Git command shows who last modified each line of a file?
questions.explanation: git blame annotates each line of a file with the commit and author that last changed it.

questions.question: Which Git command creates a new empty repository in an existing directory?
questions.explanation: git init initializes a new Git repository, creating the .git directory in the current folder.

questions.question: What is a 'detached HEAD' state in Git?
options: Checking out a specific commit instead of a branch
A branch that has no commits yet
A merge that produced unresolved conflicts
questions.explanation: Detached HEAD occurs when HEAD points directly at a commit rather than a branch, so new commits aren't on any branch.

questions.question: Which merge type simply moves the branch pointer forward when the branches have not diverged?
questions.explanation: A fast-forward merge advances the target branch pointer when there is no diverging work, creating no merge commit.

questions.question: Which Git operation combines all of a branch's commits into a single commit during a merge?
questions.explanation: git merge --squash condenses all changes from a branch into one staged change, producing a single commit.

questions.question: A developer ran 'git reset --hard HEAD~3' and lost three commits that were never pushed. Which command lists recent HEAD movements so the commits can be recovered?
questions.explanation: git reflog records every position HEAD has held; the lost commits can be restored by resetting to their reflog entry.

questions.question: main has commits A-B-C; feature branched at B and added D-E. After running 'git rebase main' while on feature, what is the result?
options: A merge commit joining C and E
D and E replayed as new commits D' and E' on top of C, with new hashes
questions.explanation: Rebase rewrites the feature commits onto the new base C, producing new SHAs (D', E') and a linear history - no merge commit.

questions.question: Which .gitignore pattern ignores every directory named 'logs' at any depth, but not regular files named 'logs'?
questions.explanation: A trailing slash restricts the pattern to directories; with no leading slash it matches 'logs' directories at any depth - files named 'logs' remain tracked.

questions.question: 'git stash' left newly created (untracked) files in the working tree. Which flag stashes them as well?
questions.explanation: 'git stash -u' includes untracked files; '--all' also adds ignored files, which is broader than needed.

questions.question: A repository ballooned to 4 GB because binaries were committed for months; the team must purge them from all history. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Add them to .gitignore and run git gc
Use git filter-repo (or BFG Repo-Cleaner) to rewrite history
questions.explanation: History rewriting tools like git filter-repo or BFG remove the binaries from every commit and shrink the object database; .gitignore only stops future commits.
